nodes.label: Automation
nodes.description: The third principle of new media, allowing operations involved in media creation, manipulation, and access to be automated, partly removing human intentionality.

nodes.label: Low-level Automation
nodes.description: Automation where users modify or create media using templates or simple algorithms, standard in commercial software like Photoshop and Word.

nodes.label: High-level Automation
nodes.description: Automation requiring a computer to understand semantics, often using AI, as seen in game AI engines or virtual actors.

nodes.label: Variability
nodes.description: The fourth principle stating a new media object can exist in infinite versions, corresponding to post-industrial 'production on demand'.

nodes.label: Scalability
nodes.description: A case of variability where versions of an object are generated at various sizes or levels of detail.

nodes.label: Hypermedia
nodes.description: A structure where media elements are connected via hyperlinks, separating elements from structure, seen as a case of variability.

nodes.label: Transcoding
nodes.description: The fifth principle where cultural categories are translated into computer's ontology, epistemology, and pragmatics.

nodes.label: Cultural Layer
nodes.description: The layer of media featuring recognizable objects, narratives, and traditional human meanings.

nodes.label: Computer Layer
nodes.description: The layer of media consisting of data structures, algorithms, variables, and machine-readable code.

nodes.label: Software Studies
nodes.description: A new stage in media theory turning to computer science to understand programmable media.

nodes.label: Cinema as Precursor
nodes.description: Cinema anticipated new media via discrete sampling of time, multimedia combinations, and random access mapping.

nodes.label: Myth of Lossless Copies
nodes.description: The notion that digital media copies identically, which is contradicted in reality by the pervasive use of lossy compression.

nodes.label: Lossy Compression
nodes.description: Techniques to reduce file size by deleting information, serving as the actual foundation of computer culture.

nodes.label: Interactivity Myth
nodes.description: The idea that 'interactive media' is unique to computers, ignoring that all HCI is interactive and older art forms required psychological interaction.

nodes.label: Externalization of Mind
nodes.description: The modern trend to objectify internal mental processes (like associations) into external visual forms or hyperlinked structures.

nodes.label: Human-Computer Interface (GUI)
nodes.description: A key semiotic code that filters all culture, imposing its own logic and blurring the work-leisure divide.
